title: Recurrence Relations & The Binomial Theorem
outcomes: Evaluate linear recursive sequences a_n = c * a_(n-1) + d iteratively from an initial condition a_1.
Apply the Binomial Theorem to extract exact coefficients of x^(n-k) in expansions of (x + c)^n.
Compute general binomial coefficients [x^(n-k)] in (ax + b)^n = C(n, k) * a^(n-k) * b^k.

sections.intuition: A recurrence relation defines each term of a sequence as a function of earlier terms, starting from an explicit base case such as a₁. Even Pascal's triangle of binomial coefficients C(n, k) is governed by the recurrence C(n, k) = C(n-1, k-1) + C(n-1, k). When expanding (ax + b)^n = (ax + b)(ax + b)...(ax + b), each term is formed by choosing b from k of the n factors and ax from the remaining (n - k) factors. Since there are C(n, k) ways to choose which k factors supply b, the x^(n-k) term is C(n, k) · (ax)^(n-k) · b^k.
sections.formal_definition:
1. First-Order Linear Recurrence: Given base case a₁ and recurrence a_n = c·a_{n-1} + d for n ≥ 2, terms are generated sequentially: a₂ = c·a₁ + d, a₃ = c·a₂ + d, and so on.
2. Binomial Theorem: For any non-negative integer n,
(ax + b)^n = ∑_{k=0}^n C(n, k) (ax)^(n-k) b^k = ∑_{k=0}^n [n! / (k!(n-k)!)] a^(n-k) b^k x^(n-k).
sections.worked_example:
Find the coefficient of x² in the expansion of (2x + 3)⁴.
1. Here n = 4 and the power of x is n - k = 2, so k = 2.
2. Compute the binomial number from Pascal's triangle: C(4, 2) = (4 × 3)/(2 × 1) = 6.
3. Raise both coefficients to their respective powers: (2x)² = 4x² and 3² = 9.
4. Multiply all three factors: 6 × 4 × 9 = 216, so the x² term is 216x².
common_misconceptions: Stopping one step early when iterating a recurrence relation (reporting a₃ instead of a₄).
Reporting only the combinatorial number C(n, k) without multiplying by the constant power c^k.
Forgetting to raise the coefficient a of (ax) to the power (n - k) when expanding (ax + b)^n.
